subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following is a physical change?
options: Melting ice
Burning magnesium
Rusting of iron
Cooking an egg
questions.explain: Melting ice changes only the state of water; no new substance is formed, so it is a physical change.

questions.q: What is the key feature that distinguishes a chemical change from a physical change?
options: One or more new substances are formed
The substance changes state
The change can always be easily reversed
Only the shape of the substance changes
questions.explain: In a chemical change the atoms are rearranged into new substances with different properties.

questions.q: Which observation is typically a sign that a chemical reaction has taken place?
options: A colour change and a gas being given off
A solid dissolving in water
Ice cream melting on a hot day
Salt water evaporating to leave salt
questions.explain: Colour changes, gas production, temperature changes and precipitate formation are signs of a chemical reaction.

questions.q: Dissolving sugar in water is best described as which type of change?
options: A physical change
A combustion reaction
A redox reaction
A neutralisation reaction
questions.explain: Dissolving sugar forms a mixture and no new substance is made, so it is a physical change that can be reversed by evaporation.

questions.q: Which of these will increase the rate of a reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Increasing the concentration of the acid
Decreasing the temperature
Using larger marble chips
Adding more water to dilute the acid
questions.explain: A higher acid concentration means more frequent collisions between reacting particles, increasing the rate.

questions.q: According to collision theory, why does increasing temperature increase the rate of reaction?
options: Particles move faster and collide more often with more energy
Particles become larger and easier to hit
The activation energy of the reaction is increased
The particles are used up more slowly
questions.explain: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so collisions are more frequent and more of them exceed the activation energy.

questions.q: What is a catalyst?
options: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction and is unchanged at the end
A substance that is used up during a reaction
A substance that increases the activation energy
A substance that slows down a reaction permanently
questions.explain: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy and is chemically unchanged afterwards.

questions.q: Why does powdering a solid reactant increase the rate of reaction compared with using a single lump?
options: It increases the surface area exposed to the other reactant
It increases the concentration of the solid
It raises the temperature of the reactants
It lowers the activation energy of the reaction
questions.explain: A larger surface area allows more collisions per second between the reactant particles, so the rate increases.

questions.q: In an experiment, 2 g of zinc powder reacts faster with acid than 2 g of a single zinc strip. The best explanation is that the powder has a:
options: Greater surface area to volume ratio
Higher concentration
Lower activation energy
Larger mass
questions.explain: The powder exposes far more surface to the acid, giving more frequent collisions and a faster rate.

questions.q: A reaction produces gas. On a graph of volume of gas against time, what does a steeper initial gradient indicate?
options: A faster initial rate of reaction
A greater total volume of gas produced
A slower rate of reaction
That the reaction has stopped
questions.explain: The gradient of a volume-time graph represents the rate, so a steeper slope means a faster reaction.

questions.q: Which symbol is used to represent a reversible reaction?
questions.explain: The two half arrows (⇌) show that the reaction can proceed in both the forward and backward directions.

questions.q: When anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is used to test for water, the colour change observed is:
options: White to blue
Blue to white
Pink to blue
Colourless to purple
questions.explain: Adding water to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate forms blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate, a reversible reaction used to test for water.

questions.q: At dynamic equilibrium in a closed system, which statement is correct?
options: The forward and backward reactions occur at the same rate
The forward reaction has stopped completely
There are no more reactant molecules left
The backward reaction is faster than the forward reaction
questions.explain: At equilibrium both reactions continue but at equal rates, so the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant.

questions.q: Which balanced equation represents the Haber process for making ammonia?
options: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
N₂ + H₂ ⇌ NH₃
2N + 3H ⇌ NH₃
N₂ + 2H₂ ⇌ 2NH₂
questions.explain: Nitrogen and hydrogen react in a 1:3 ratio to form ammonia in the reversible Haber process.

questions.q: In the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, forward reaction exothermic), increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to:
options: The right, increasing the yield of ammonia
The left, decreasing the yield of ammonia
Neither side, as pressure has no effect
The left, forming more nitrogen and hydrogen only
questions.explain: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules (2 molecules of ammonia versus 4 of reactants), increasing ammonia yield.

questions.q: In terms of electrons, oxidation is defined as:
options: Loss of electrons
Gain of electrons
Gain of protons
Loss of neutrons
questions.explain: Using OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons.

questions.q: In the reaction 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, which species is oxidised?
options: Magnesium, because it gains oxygen
Oxygen, because it gains electrons
Magnesium oxide, because it loses electrons
Oxygen, because it loses oxygen
questions.explain: Magnesium gains oxygen and loses electrons to form Mg²⁺, so it is oxidised.

questions.q: What is the role of an oxidising agent in a redox reaction?
options: It gains electrons and is itself reduced
It loses electrons and is itself oxidised
It neither gains nor loses electrons
It only provides oxygen and is unchanged
questions.explain: An oxidising agent oxidises another species by taking its electrons, so the agent is itself reduced.

questions.q: Acidified potassium manganate(VII) is used as a test for a reducing agent. What colour change confirms a reducing agent is present?
options: Purple to colourless
Colourless to purple
Orange to green
Blue to white
questions.explain: A reducing agent reduces the purple manganate(VII) ions, decolourising the solution.

questions.q: In the reaction Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, which statement is correct?
options: Zinc is oxidised and copper ions are reduced
Zinc is reduced and copper ions are oxidised
Both zinc and copper are oxidised
Neither species undergoes a change in oxidation state
questions.explain: Zinc loses electrons (oxidised) to form Zn²⁺, while Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons (reduced) to form copper metal.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry (0620) syllabus; Chemical Reactions
